correspondence.component_scope: Chosen eastern unnamed feeder, westward collecting corridor and Truxton join
correspondence.finding: The regional original maps the chosen eastern opening on an unnamed intermittent feeder. This channel runs southwest across the road corridor, turns west along the railway valley, and joins the mapped Truxton Wash corridor coming from the south. The regional original retains this minor-channel linework where the more detailed display omits it. The private enlarged reading of the successful original establishes the opening and through-join at ordinary corridor scale; no nearby name is substituted for the connection.
correspondence.name_scope: Unnamed selected feeder and its join to the separately named receiving Truxton Wash.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper named Truxton Wash through the Peach Springs–Truxton corridor
correspondence.finding: The mapped wash continues west and then southwest beneath repeated Truxton Wash labels. The valley bends, lateral gullies, road and railway setting, and onward passage toward Crozier are continuously depicted. Small adjacent stock waters are not treated as selected through-lake transfers.

The detail original depicts the selected southbound corridor through the Crozier and Valentine setting, with repeated Truxton Wash labels and visible entering side drainages, including the Wright Canyon setting. It connects the upper southwest wash directly to the southern bend; no intervening lake, glacier or engineered transfer is needed.
correspondence.name_scope: Truxton Wash confined middle corridor; side valleys remain distinct.

correspondence.component_scope: Southern bend, Hackberry tributary junction and northwest turn
correspondence.finding: The named Truxton Wash follows the valley around the southern bend east of Hackberry, receives the separately labeled southern Hackberry Wash, and turns northwest between the mountain fronts. The overview and middle detail show the actual corridor and junction, rather than mere basin proximity.
correspondence.name_scope: Truxton Wash remains the selected receiving corridor; Hackberry Wash is a distinct unselected tributary.

correspondence.component_scope: Northwest lower valley and Hualapai Valley collecting wash
correspondence.finding: The selected course follows the mapped wash northwest out of the confined valley and then west across the wider alluvial valley. Repeated Truxton Wash labels, intermittent channels and broad mapped wash surfaces establish the continuous collecting corridor through the intervening side-drainage joins. The cartographic transition between dotted channel and wider dry-wash depiction is not a source gap.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower northwest approach and southern Red Lake entry
correspondence.finding: The terminal original follows the named Truxton Wash northwest and then north to the southern margin of the mapped playa. This is one continuous receiving corridor, also shown and named on ADWR Figure 1. No extension north toward Hualapai Wash or Lake Mead is part of the selected route.
correspondence.name_scope: Truxton Wash terminal approach; Red Lake is the receiving playa.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual terminal playa and final selected ending
correspondence.finding: The final selected parts enter and end inside the same broad playa polygon reached from the south by Truxton Wash. ADWR Figure 1 explicitly names this waterbody Red Lake. The USGSTopo stippled dry-lake depiction supplies the terminal geographic setting. A continuous river line across the playa floor, a precise wetted thread or current standing water is not required for this correspondence.
correspondence.name_scope: Red Lake terminal playa, separate from the representative wash name.

correspondence.finding: The chosen northern opening lies in a south-trending mountain valley. The same dry collector can be followed through constrictions and wider gravel/alluvial reaches, with short lateral washes arriving from the bordering ridges. No neighbouring western valley is substituted.

The valley broadens into a southward fan with several distributary-looking dry threads. An eastern alluvial arrival merges with the same low receiving fan. The selected coarse segments stay within this continuous valley-to-fan setting.

The feeder fan reaches the pale salt-flat margin, then the selected continuation bends west along the northeastern receiving floor below rocky upland spurs. The fan entry and saline receiving setting are visible continuously; a named river channel across the flat is not inferred.

The selected southwestward continuation lies within the same broad open salar, adjacent to western rocky ridges and coalescing marginal fans. Saline bands and fan surfaces connect this sector with the northeastern entry; no intervening separate basin or ridge transfer is observed.

The continuation proceeds southwest beside the western mountain margin while remaining on the connected salt-flat floor. Lateral fans spread into this same receiving area. Road-like crossings are not treated as channels or hydraulic infrastructure.

The selected end turns east across the lower interior of the same broad receiving salar. Clouds and mosaic differences obscure some surface detail, but the surrounding continuous floor and flanking mountain margins establish its receiving setting. No precise stream trace across the salt floor, current flow or transfer to another basin is claimed.

correspondence.component_scope: Western selected opening and first forested feeder interval
correspondence.finding: The selected opening falls in the depicted continuous western feeder approaching the Río Estrella reach. Drainage linework, the thematic tributary pattern and imagery valley setting account for the through-link. No named spring, precise source point or universal name for the tiny headward interval is asserted.

correspondence.component_scope: Southwestern feeder and its northeast approach to the Clarito-side junction
correspondence.finding: The basin map labels the southwestern feeder Río Estrella. The selected route approaches from this branch, then joins the eastward river near the Clarito/Nueva Zelandia setting. Río Clarito is an entering contextual tributary, not a representative alias.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastward upper continuation to its joining Río Changuinola
correspondence.finding: MiAmbiente explicitly labels the downstream eastward reach Río Estrellita and depicts its junction with north-flowing Río Changuinola. Lajas and Ceiba enter the surrounding network but are not substituted for the selected route. The service raster accounts for the intermediate joins and the eastern northward turn.

correspondence.component_scope: Northward receiving reach from Estrellita through the Culubre-side junction
correspondence.finding: The mapped Changuinola corridor continues north past the Culubre entry toward Peña Blanca. The selected route stays on Changuinola; the separately named Culubre tributary is not selected upstream.

correspondence.component_scope: Inundated middle-valley passage, dam site and downstream outlet corridor
correspondence.finding: Imagery continuously covers the selected reservoir passage and downstream valley. IMHPA places Central Hidroeléctrica Changuinola I on this river and its Sitio de Presa I station at the corresponding dam setting. Changuinola I is retained as infrastructure identity, not an asserted formal lake name. No transfer across another basin or unseen tunnel is needed to account for the selected valley route.

correspondence.component_scope: Dam-side downstream continuation, Valle del Risco, lower meanders and the stage3-to-stage2 fragment join
correspondence.finding: Original imagery and basin cartography continuously cover the downstream river and the join between both selected mainstem fragments. ETESA station prose corroborates the Culubre–Peña Blanca–Valle del Risco–Teribe order. The Teribe confluence is a contextual joining tributary, not an additional selected FID.

correspondence.component_scope: Teribe-side lower valley, Changuinola alluvial plain, estuary and actual Caribbean ending
correspondence.finding: The selected lower river follows the visible channel through the coastal plain and reaches the open Caribbean mouth shown by the imagery and basin map. Both the stored source ending and the distinct displayed coastal extension lie in this same mouth/receiving-sea setting; exact shoreline positions are not asserted.

Loreto’s Relieve original depicts the selected short eastern opening in the inland mountain drainage south of Cerro El Gamusita. The initial northern and westward bends enter the same connected valley that continues toward Santa Cruz. The nearby east-draining coastal channels are separate. The chosen model opening is not asserted to be the officially recognized source or to have a individually verified hydronym.

The Loreto original directly labels Santa Cruz on the westward valley followed by the selection. It depicts the valley bending southwest to the Comondú boundary; the complementary Comondú original continues that same drainage into the western foothills. This correspondence uses the actual connected linework and terrain, rather than municipal or basin membership alone.

Comondú depicts the selected southwestern descent and successive joining feeder channels through the foothills, east and south of the separately labeled El Huatamote tributary. The selected course reaches the broad southern alluvial bend before turning northwest. The plain imagery corroborates the lower half of this connected dry-valley approach and its receiving alluvial setting. No separate hydronym is securely assigned to this entire intervening reach.

The Comondú original places Querétaro on the northwestern receiving leg after the southern turn. The original imagery shows that the selected approach and northwestern leg occupy one continuous broad alluvial wash along the agricultural margin. Joining fans and branching dry channels are visible. The correspondence does not depend on a presently wetted thread or a precise bank match.

Comondú directly labels La Peña on the western continuation; the northern part of the 2019 integrated-study maps depicts the same lower drainage and its surrounding tributaries. The two overlapping imagery views show the continuous wash through and around cultivated fields, across the north-south road corridor, and around its northward bend to the receiving northern channel. Agricultural roads and fields do not require an unexplained transfer to a different valley at the scale of this finding. Present diversion, irrigation or flood-control operations are not established.

The selected southern plain corridor joins the northern receiving drainage near Santo Domingo and follows the broad northwestward and then southwestward lower bend. The integrated study’s Map 4.2 directly labels Santo Domingo on this lower reach. The 1996 hydrological study independently identifies the Santo Domingo river and its coastal outlet, while the imagery depicts the actual receiving join and continuously connected lower valley. The study’s principal upper-source narrative is not substituted for the distinct selected Santa Cruz opening.

The western selected reach enters a continuously depicted tidal channel and coastal wetland, with vegetated flats, open-water branches and an inlet through the coastal barrier farther west. The actual stored endpoint is within this connected Santo Domingo estuarine receiving setting, rather than at the ocean side of the barrier. The distinct underlying source endpoint and displayed endpoint both remain in that same receiving setting at ordinary scale; they are not treated as identical points. No extra extension to the Pacific inlet is made part of the selection. The historical maps identify the Santo Domingo outlet, and the original terminal imagery closes the final tidal correspondence.

The inspected selection is an arid mountain-stream, alluvial-plain and tidal-estuary corridor, without a selected glacier, named inland lake or mapped major reservoir passage. Cultivated land borders and locally crosses the dry drainage setting, while the estuary includes vegetated tidal flats. The nearby El Ihuajil reservoir and Las Bramonas drainage belong to the separate southern system and are not inserted into this path.
